Conventional image segmentation techniques typically rely on manual annotations and large annotated datasets, which are often costly and time-intensive to produce. Self-supervised learning (SSL) offers a promising alternative by utilizing unlabeled data to train models; however, its application in medical imaging remains limited due to the inherent complexity of automatically learning meaningful representations from such data. To address this, we introduce Boundary-Sensitive Information Optimization (BSIO), a novel framework designed to enhance self-supervised medical image segmentation. Specifically, we develop a boundary-aware contrastive learning method that extracts robust representations by leveraging boundary-sensitive information. Furthermore, we propose a boundary information optimization module that refines segmentation outcomes by effectively integrating these SSL-derived representations with unlabeled boundary data. Experiments conducted on two datasets demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance, surpassing existing self-supervised and semi-supervised approaches.

We introduce Intents and Theory-of-Mind (ITM), a novel framework designed to enhance the capabilities of AI agents in open-ended, multi-agent environments. We argue that current approaches often fall short in these settings because they lack the ability to establish and maintain coherent long-term objectives, as well as to anticipate the intentions and beliefs of other participants. In response, we define Intent as the mechanism by which an AI agent formulates and adheres to sustained goals, while Theory-of-Mind represents the formulation of hypotheses regarding the intentions and mental states of other agents. We validate ITM by applying it to the role-playing game Dungeons and Dragons (D&D), creating a specialized D&D Dungeon Master (DMM) agent guided by this model. This agent was evaluated using a human-in-the-loop methodology against a baseline DMM trained on standard large language models. The results indicate that DMMs equipped with ITM were perceived by human players as more engaging, effective leaders, and possessing greater social intelligence.

Although it is a fundamental aspect of human language, the phenomenon of lexical semantic shift—where word meanings evolve over time—remains difficult to study. We propose a new methodology for capturing these changes by analyzing diachronic variations in word collocations. This approach tracks how associations with other words fluctuate across different historical periods. To validate our method, we conducted experiments on English using a corpus of one million sentences from the year 1800 as a baseline. Our analysis successfully identified 1,000 words exhibiting measurable collocation shifts between 1800 and 2000. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these automatic discoveries align with a manually curated list of 1,000 words known to have undergone semantic change, achieving an F1 score of 0.69.

This paper introduces the concept of transverse-momentum-dependent (quasi)parton distribution functions defined via light-cone correlation functions involving two nucleon states, where one is a quasi-nucleon and the other is either a nucleon or also a quasi-nucleon. We demonstrate that integrating these functions over transverse momentum yields familiar unpolarized and polarizing functions for the case of a single nucleon. Furthermore, we establish the theoretical framework for their renormalization and evolution. Specifically, we prove that the $k_\perp$-dependent functions derived from quasi-nucleon states evolve according to the CCFM equation, whereas those from the mixed quasi-nucleon/nucleon configuration satisfy the DGLAP equation.

Proteins often fold into topologically intricate structures, with knotted proteins representing a particularly intriguing subset. While the native topological state of a protein constrains its folding trajectory, the specific mechanisms by which knots form and are selected remain elusive. This study introduces a novel method to identify the formation pathways of protein knots directly from their native structures. By analyzing the evolution of a knot's complexity, we identified that the number of crossings in a knot's minimal diagram increases monotonically along any physically plausible deformation path leading to the protein's unfolded state. Consequently, we propose a selection criterion for topological deformations: any process that reduces knot complexity must be deemed non-physical. Applying this framework to three distinct protein knots, we successfully reconstructed their knot formation pathways by utilizing known molecular dynamics (MD) simulation data.

We present a new analysis of Early Dark Energy (EDE) constraints derived from Planck and BOSS data, utilizing profile likelihood methods. This approach offers a robust framework for incorporating diverse datasets and parameters, enabling the assessment of how datasets interact and influence the likelihood of models with multiple parameters. Our findings indicate that profile likelihood analysis yields constraints on EDE consistent with those obtained via the traditional method of varying parameters individually. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the profile likelihood method effectively captures the negative correlation between the EDE fraction and the effective number of neutrino species ($N_{\rm eff}$) observed in the joint Planck and BOSS analysis.

We introduce the definition of symplectic mapping type groups for a specific category of torus submanifolds that result from blowups. Our findings demonstrate that these groups are finitely generated, possess a finite presentation, and are generated by Dehn and positive德拉姆 (Drum) drag operations. Additionally, we establish an isomorphism between the mapping type group of a single torus blowup and that of a rational complex structure on the corresponding Fano manifold, assuming the existence of such a structure in the same cohomology class.

The Nambu-Goldstone theorem, which links spontaneous symmetry breaking to the emergence of massless Nambu-Goldstone bosons, is a cornerstone of both relativistic and non-relativistic quantum field theories. This work examines the conditions required for spontaneous symmetry breaking and the subsequent emergence of these bosons within various frameworks, including relativistic theories, Galilean-invariant theories, and those featuring relativistic symmetries broken down to Lorentz invariance. We demonstrate that the standard form of the theorem holds true for relativistic cases, whereas the presence of Galilean invariance necessitates a revised formulation. Furthermore, we establish that whenever a global internal symmetry is spontaneously broken in a theory retaining Lorentz symmetry, the standard theorem applies; however, if Lorentz symmetry is also broken, the standard theorem must be replaced by a modified version.

Counterfactual explanations are vital for fostering trust in AI, yet current methods often fail to provide the necessary context for users to comprehend model behavior. To address this, we introduce DISCO, a novel framework that utilizes large language models to generate contextualized, phrase-level counterfactuals. By leveraging contextual information, these outputs offer more intuitive insights into model predictions. We evaluated DISCO across various tasks, including fact-checking, machine reading comprehension, and natural language inference, demonstrating that it significantly outperforms existing methods.
This paper investigates complete fair and neighborhood sum distinguishing total colorings specifically applied to certain circulant graph types.

We introduce a strategy utilizing a pinhole-pierced graphene membrane to govern the growth of Heusler films on sapphire substrates. This approach enables the transition from remote epitaxy, characterized by lattice mismatch, to van der Waals epitaxy by gradually aligning the film's lattice parameters with those of the substrate. This regulation is achieved by adjusting the tensile stress within the graphene layer via substrate curvature manipulation. Employing the Co2MnSi/Co2MnGe/Co2MnGa system as a model, we demonstrate that this method allows for the continuous tuning of the structural and magnetic properties of the resulting Heusler films.

A linear code $C$ qualifies as a $\mathbb{Z}_p\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}$-linear code when it is an additive code over the ring $R_{p^2} = \mathbb{Z}_p\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}$ whose generator matrix exhibits a specific block structure. This paper investigates the dimensions of such codes and their associated null spaces.

Ideal polymer plugs are created by solving the governing equations of flow and polymer degradation under the assumption of an instantaneous transition between the TRL states. These solutions are applied to analyze the optimal injection history for a polymer plug within a linear reservoir, subject to constraints on total fluid volume and time. The resulting time-minimal injection profiles consist of two phases: an initial period of constant polymer concentration, followed by a phase governed by a time-dependent concentration determined by an adjoint variable. The study also examines how these profiles are affected by variations in the reservoir's mobility and the Damkohler number.

Positive unlabeled (PU) learning addresses scenarios where only data containing a target concept and unlodata are available. While existing methods typically yield a single positive class label per instance, these approaches often fall short when dealing with multiple possible positive labels for one instance. To address this gap, we propose a novel framework for extracting multi-label positives from single positive inputs. Our method leverages a knowledge graph to map concept labels to their corresponding entities, utilizing concept-level predictions to derive multi-label instances. Experiments on two datasets demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms standard multi-instance learning (MIL) techniques.

This paper examines the time-fractional Cahn-Allen equation, defined by $\partial_t^\alpha u(t,x)=\Delta u(t,x)+u(t,x)+u^3(t,x)$, where the fractional derivative $\partial_t^\alpha$ is of order $0<\alpha<2$. By establishing a diminishing upper energy bound applicable to this fractional equation, we derive the asymptotic behavior of its solutions.

We demonstrate that the correspondence between algebraic observables and physical states in a rigid symmetric monoidal category and the data comprising a HSP framework forms an adjunction of 2-categories. Specifically, we identify the category of HSP data as the left adjoint and the 2-category of rigid symmetric monoidal categories as the right adjoint. Furthermore, we establish a separate adjunction of 2-categories focusing specifically on the mapping between algebras of observables and state systems.

We investigate the high-energy emission of radio galaxies powered by supermassive black holes that accrete via magnetized disks. In this model, magnetic fields emerge from the disk and are transported outward by magnetic buoyancy, eventually becoming trapped in the surrounding accretion flow. These fields generate gamma-rays through inverse Compton scattering of soft photons from the central engine. Our simulations indicate that these sources can emit gamma-rays up to 10 TeV, with the maximum energy scaling with the black hole's spin. The model also predicts a hard X-ray component and non-thermal synchrotron radio emission, both of which align with observational data. Furthermore, the predicted spectral energy distributions resemble those of active galactic nuclei fueled by advection-dominated accretion flows, suggesting that magnetic-capture disks represent a more prevalent accretion mechanism than standard models.

This study examines the allocation of portfolio returns across cross-sections, analyzing the relationships between return dispersion, return dispersion, and the Sharpe ratio. It evaluates various portfolio construction approaches, including mean-variance optimization, factor models, and machine learning techniques, to determine how these methods influence the portfolio's ability to achieve the cross-sectional correlation.

This study introduces an automatic heart sound classification system designed to detect additive noise and implement deformations within Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). While CNNs have established themselves as a leading solution for medical image and signal classification, their susceptibility to data distribution shifts in the wild remains a challenge. To address this, we propose a framework that integrates two specific techniques: (1) the incorporation of additive white Gaussian noise during training to simulate background noise, and (2) the utilization of Convolutional Deformation (ConvDeform) layers to handle variations in signal length and shape. Experiments conducted on a dataset of heart sounds collected from real-world environments demonstrate that this combined framework achieves a 90.1% accuracy rate, surpassing a standard baseline CNN by 1.5%.

The proliferation of wearable devices capable of gathering extensive health data has significantly improved the accuracy of disease diagnosis and treatment. Nevertheless, uploading this sensitive data to centralized servers creates substantial privacy risks. Although existing federated learning approaches mitigate these concerns, they often overlook the heterogeneity of device capabilities and the diversity of data distributions. To address these challenges, we propose **FedHealth**, a novel framework that integrates transfer learning within a federated setting. This solution enables the aggregation of information from non-identical sources to deliver robust disease classification models. Specifically, our method employs a two-stage strategy: initially, a baseline model is pre-trained on abundant source domain data; subsequently, this model is fine-tuned using limited target domain data. Furthermore, to accommodate varying label scarcity across clients, we introduce a flexible transfer mechanism that dynamically adjusts the amount of transferred information. Extensive experiments utilizing real-world data from Fitbit wearables demonstrate that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance, particularly excelling in scenarios characterized by limited target domain labels.

This paper introduces a novel approach to portfolio optimization that replaces traditional mean-variance methods with an alternative framework. This new model relies on a skewness and kurtosis-based risk measure and incorporates skewness, kurtosis, and expected return as objective functions. By transforming this setup into a multi-objective problem, the researchers first reduce it to a single-objective linear program. The resulting model is then converted into a multi-period portfolio optimization task using the equivalent linear program. Finally, numerical experiments are conducted to evaluate the method's performance.

The coincidence dilemma, first described by M. B. Finan and the author in 2001, highlights a tension between two approaches to modeling coincidences: the objective, data-driven method of the Poisson process and the subjective, event-driven nature of the gamma process. While the gamma process offers flexibility by allowing model parameters to be updated with every observed event, it risks overfitting due to its high dimensionality. In contrast, the Poisson process, with its constraint of a fixed rate, provides a more parsimonious fit. This paper introduces a new model that bridges this divide by defining a stochastic rate process with a discrete-time Markov structure. By utilizing a discrete-time, discrete-space stochastic framework, the authors demonstrate that the proposed process is both parsimonious and statistically consistent with gamma process characteristics.

This work presents an automated system designed to handle user submissions in programming contests. It details the implementation of a robust testing framework and a modular solution architecture, which together enable rapid integration of new problem types. Additionally, it outlines the deployment of this framework on a specific online contest platform.

This paper examines the toggling control problem involving investment adjustments and investment expenses, where expenses are defined as càdlàg (right-continuous with limits) functions of the timing of changes. The authors derive necessary conditions for optimal strategies using dynamic programming and analyze their long-term behavior. They demonstrate that the problem admits an asymptotically optimal approach characterized by a finite number of toggles. Furthermore, the paper establishes a connection between this specific toggling issue and the classical Merton problem.

The proposed leptoquark (LQ) extension of the Standard Model (SM) posits that these leptoquarks arise as an accidental feature. This study examines the LHC's potential to detect LQs, focusing on the role of uneven LQ pair production. Specifically, we analyze scenarios where production rates for the two LQ types differ significantly, such as a mass ratio of $m_{LQ1}/m_{LQ2} \approx 2$. We find that even a substantial mass disparity does not hinder the LHC's ability to identify both LQs, provided the lighter LQ has a mass below approximately 1.5 TeV.

Educators frequently employ brief, high-dimensional temporal sequences (such as those found in True/False or multiple-choice formats) to evaluate student comprehension of life sciences. However, automated scoring of these questions remains challenging because students may guess the correct answer without genuine understanding. To address this, we propose a novel sequential classification model designed to predict student performance on these items. This approach utilizes a bidirectional long short-term memory (LSTM) network to process answer choices and associated metadata sequentially. By integrating sequential processing with deep learning, the model effectively captures complex, non-linear relationships between the data and performance outcomes. Furthermore, we introduce a new, efficient algorithm for training these networks on sequential inputs. Experiments conducted on a dataset of 1.2 million records demonstrate that this proposed model significantly outperforms traditional statistical methods and existing deep learning baselines.

We examine the subthermal excitation of molecular gas reservoirs in galaxies, a mechanism where the local critical density ($n_{\rm cr}$) exceeds the ambient interstellar medium density, causing the energy input from stellar UV radiation to dominate over thermal heating. This study focuses on the rotational transitions of neutral carbon (C {\sc i}) within these molecules, which are typically too weak to be detected. However, our findings indicate that under subthermal conditions, C {\sc i} lines can reach sufficient intensities to be observable. We utilize a one-dimensional model of molecular gas to simulate the subthermal environment, incorporating the effects of UV radiation on the rotational states of bound electrons in C {\sc i} lines. Our simulations reveal that the C {\sc i} $^3P_1$ and $^3P_2$ transitions can achieve intensities comparable to those of the $^3P_0$ lines, which are already known to be detectable. Furthermore, the model demonstrates that the C {\sc i} $^3P_1$ and $^3P_2$ lines exhibit a strong dependence on UV radiation field intensity, whereas the $^3P_0$ line remains largely insensitive to such variations. Consequently, the ratio of the $^3P_1$ line intensity to the $^3P_0$ line intensity serves as a sensitive diagnostic tool for determining the ambient UV radiation field within molecular gas.

We propose a model of vector-like quarks that simultaneously addresses recent tensions in $B$-meson decay anomalies and the direct CP violation in Kaon decays ($\epsilon_K$). This framework generates the required effective operators through tree-level exchanges of two neutral singlets and one neutral triplet, comprising both real and complex scalar fields. The model successfully accounts for the observed anomalies via contributions to rare charmless $b \to s \ell^+ \ell^-$ transitions and $B \to K^{(*)} \ell^+ \ell^-$ rare three-body decays, while simultaneously generating the required CP-violating phase in the kaon system.

This paper investigates the series reconstruction problem for Hamming distance within the context of arrangement codes. We establish that the problem is resolvable for codes defined by a binary Hamming distance of 2, whereas it remains unresolved for all other parameter combinations.

This study introduces a hierarchical few-shot learning framework designed to enhance musical instrument recognition. In this approach, prototypes are established for each class using few-shot learning techniques. These prototypes are then employed to identify intermediate categories, such as strings, winds, or percussion groups, creating an intermediate classification layer. Finally, these intermediate categories facilitate the identification of specific target classes. Experiments conducted within the MIDI Instrument Classification Challenge (MICC) environment demonstrate that this hierarchical framework achieves a 10.5% improvement in the challenge's few-shot learning task compared to a strong baseline.

We introduce an open-access dataset comprising 1,000 question-answer pairs derived from 250 research articles. Our dataset is designed to facilitate the evaluation of question-answering systems, particularly in scenarios where answers are grounded in extended passages or documents. We define and assess three specific answer types: (1) sub-document spans, (2) explicit information within the text, and (3) implicit information requiring inference. To support this, we establish corresponding evaluation metrics for each category. Additionally, we release a benchmark that aggregates results from eleven state-of-the-art question-answering models using our dataset.

Pulsar timing array (PTA) observations are increasingly sensitive to gravitational waves from inspiralling elliptical binaries, necessitating the use of full post-Newtonian (PN) precision to accurately model these signals. We analyze the spectral characteristics of PTA signals generated by such binaries across various PN orders, comparing them against both the standard quadrupole approximation and the full 3.5PN formalism. Our analysis reveals that while the quadrupole formula suffices to distinguish a single source from the stochastic background, the 1PN correction significantly enhances the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and improves the accuracy of inferred source parameters. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the 3.5PN model is required to effectively separate two overlapping sources from the galactic background. Our findings indicate that the spectral features of elliptical binaries are highly sensitive to the waveform's PN order; consequently, employing a model that lacks full PN precision can lead to substantial biases in the recovered source parameters. Finally, we assess the computational costs associated with these models, showing that the 3.5PN formulation incurs only a marginal increase in expense compared to the quadrupole model.

The rapid dissemination of infectious agents, such as SARS-CoV-2, demands mathematical models capable of capturing outbreak dynamics. This paper examines the foundational principles of compartmental modelling, specifically the SIR framework, and explores model extensions that incorporate vaccination, latent infection, and mobility constraints. We highlight how SIR models and their derivatives offer a practical tool for estimating key epidemiological metrics, including the basic reproduction number ($R_0$) and effective reproduction number ($R_t$), as well as projecting infection trajectories and peak loads. Furthermore, we discuss the integration of model outputs with empirical data to inform public health strategies and policy decisions.

We examine the Shannon entropy and linear majorization metrics for Majorana fermions across a spectrum of thermal states, contrasting these findings with those of canonical bosonic and Boltzmann-gas systems. Our analysis indicates that, at identical temperatures, Shannon entropy and linear majorization within a thermal environment yield strictly greater disorder for a Majorana gas relative to a Boltzmann gas or a bosonic gas. Furthermore, we establish that thermal states composed of Majorana particles exhibit greater disorder than their zero-temperature counterparts. Finally, we demonstrate that, at any given temperature, a thermal ensemble of Majorana gas exhibits higher disorder than a thermal ensemble of blackbody radiation.

Acronyms are a common feature in technical writing, serving as space-saving alternatives for frequently used phrases. However, understanding an acronym requires knowing its specific expansion, which can vary by context. This study introduces MadDog, a system that gathers evidence from diverse sources to identify acronyms and resolve their ambiguities. MadDog operates in two stages: it first constructs a comprehensive database of acronyms and their meanings, then utilizes this collection to detect acronyms within text and assign the correct expansions based on context. To build this database, the approach leverages existing tools and creates a new method for discovering acronyms through morphological analysis. Furthermore, the paper outlines a new approach for integrating this rich dataset to effectively disambiguate acronyms using contextual information. Experiments demonstrate that MadDog successfully identifies acronyms with high precision and recall, while also achieving strong performance in providing accurate expansions.

The coherent conversion of ultracold atom pairs into bound molecular states offers a pathway to explore exotic quantum phases, such as the Fermi-Hubbard model, by facilitating strong dimer-dimer interactions. This study demonstrates that such interactions can be achieved using two spin-polarized fermionic lithium atoms confined in an optical trap. By applying a laser tuned to resonate with the three-body recombination channel, we show the creation of a dimer-bound state from two atoms in the spin-up configuration. Furthermore, we investigate the dynamics of this atom-to-molecule transformation, analyzing how interaction strengths and detuning levels influence the process.

DNA data storage has emerged as a promising solution for addressing the escalating global demand for memory, offering a theoretical density of 215 petabytes per liter. To achieve this, synthetic DNA sequences are generated using enzymatic reactions that assemble oligonucleotides into longer strands. However, current enzymatic synthesis methods suffer from high error rates, creating complex patterns of insertions, deletions, and substitutions. These mistakes frequently result in hierarchical structures within stored data, necessitating costly and computationally intensive correction algorithms. This study introduces a novel, efficient algorithm designed to automatically identify and rectify common insertions and deletions. By automating the repair process, the approach simplifies the management of DNA storage systems, reduces the computational burden on users, and allows for more effective system maintenance.

Topological insulators and related topological phases in condensed matter physics are frequently characterized by topological nodal surfaces in real space, which include Hopf links, tori, and higher-genus surfaces. While these real-space structures are significant, their counterparts in momentum space have long been recognized as mathematically equivalent and are topologically classified by the same invariants. Recently, topological nodal surfaces in momentum space have been realized in photonic systems, magnetic systems, and topological crystalline insulators. This review examines the classification of these momentum-space surfaces, analyzes their recent experimental realizations, and explores the connections between real-space and momentum-space topological phases.

Brain tumors represent a prevalent and perilous neurological disorder, necessitating precise diagnosis and treatment planning. Deep learning has emerged as a potent tool for automating the classification and segmentation of these tumors. Nevertheless, current deep learning architectures often require substantial computational resources and may overlook critical tumor details. Addressing these limitations, we propose Multi-Affinity Guided NetWork (MAG-Net), a bi-task framework designed for simultaneous brain tumor classification and segmentation. Our approach incorporates three key innovations: (1) Multi-Task Focus Directed Blocks (MTFDB), which facilitate feature sharing to enhance classification and segmentation performance; (2) a Multi-Affinity Guided (MAG) attention mechanism that isolates tumor regions by aggregating features from multiple levels and channels; and (3) a Multi-Affinity Guided Skip Connection (MAGSC) that refines low-level details by integrating high-level semantic information. Evaluated on the BraTS 2019 dataset, MAG-Net achieves Dice Similarity Coefficients (DSC) of 0.911 for segmentation and 0.998 for classification. Furthermore, it outperforms several state-of-the-art models, demonstrating superior efficiency with a computational time of 0.051 seconds.

Inverse problems, such as those involving control, inverse Stefan problems, or image deblurring, frequently involve regularization to ensure well-posedness. This study introduces a novel, highly adaptable regularization technique that integrates differentiable shadow evaluation with the evaluation of a differentiable sensitivity matrix. By leveraging these components, the approach yields a differentiable regularization method applicable to a broad spectrum of inverse problems. We demonstrate the technique's versatility by applying it to various problems, including image restoration, control issues, and inverse Stefan problems. Furthermore, we establish the convergence of the proposed algorithm and validate its efficacy through multiple numerical experiments.

Interlaced video remains a prevalent legacy format, yet its inherent scanning artifacts degrade visual quality, particularly during motion. Existing approaches to address this issue include hardware-based solutions, which are constrained by hardware-specific limitations, and traditional algorithms that often rely on multiple frames, introducing unacceptable latency for real-time applications. Although recent methods utilizing frame interpolation can achieve deep-fake level results using just two frames, they remain unsuitable for scenarios involving only a single frame. This paper introduces a new technique for deep video deinterlacing that utilizes only instantaneous frames, enabling high-quality reconstruction with minimal latency. Our approach generates two progressive frames from a single input by employing a generator network trained on interlaced video data. We also present a new loss function designed to enhance the structural integrity of generated content. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that our method surpasses current state-of-the-art approaches.

Numerical simulations of the Shallow Water Equations (SWE) are essential for modeling geophysical fluid dynamics, yet they remain computationally demanding. This study introduces a deep learning-based solver designed to solve the time-dependent SWE with high efficiency. By employing a U-Net convolutional neural network architecture, the model is trained to predict flow depth and current velocity at subsequent time steps using initial conditions and current flow data. The training dataset comprises over 10 million flow realizations generated via a traditional numerical solver across various initial states and parameters. Results indicate that the proposed solver achieves prediction errors below 1% for depth and velocity when tested on unseen data, while accelerating solution times by a factor of 100 compared to conventional methods.

High-dynamic-range (HDR) imaging is achieved by merging multiple exposures to expand a scene's dynamic range, a method essential for mobile devices where single-shot sensor dynamic range is limited. This study introduces an HDR framework that autonomously selects exposures and merges them, enabling seamless HDR capture without user intervention. The proposed system utilizes a simplified yet effective model for exposure choice, determining parameters through a numerical optimization process. Additionally, a new tone-mapping method is proposed to combine exposures, offering a computationally efficient alternative to complex gradient-domain techniques. Extensive experiments validate the method's efficacy, demonstrating superior performance compared to existing approaches.

We introduce a new approach to the training of neural networks with a cyclic architecture, designed to produce behavior governed by a specified directed acyclic graph (DAG). Unlike prior methods, our technique requires no pre-training and avoids the use of reinforcement learning. Instead, it relies on cyclic gradient descent, which naturally minimizes cyclic interference costs. We demonstrate that this strategy effectively approximates the minimal cost pathways highlighted by the target DAG. Our analysis extends to scenarios where networks are trained using various loss functions, including those incorporating human feedback.

The thermal profile within a stationary fluidized bed is determined using magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to examine heat distribution patterns and their evolution over time. This non-invasive experimental setup allows for the temperature mapping of a heated granular layer at 20 Hz, revealing that the layer's thickness fluctuates at this frequency. These oscillations are attributed to variations in the material's dielectric properties, specifically the longitudinal relaxation time ($T_1$), rather than actual temperature changes. Consequently, relying solely on $T_1$ data for temperature assessment introduces significant inaccuracies. To address this, a calibration method is developed that incorporates both $T_1$ and the transverse relaxation time ($T_2$) to generate precise temperature maps.

This paper explores the connection between the b-principle and the feeble Mumford hypothesis. We demonstrate that the feeble Mumford hypothesis is equivalent to the assertion that the b-principle holds for all varieties $X$ admitting a very ample line bundle $L$ with $h^i(X,L^{\otimes j})=0$ for all $i>0$ and $j\geq 1$. Furthermore, we establish a criterion for verifying the feeble Mumford hypothesis, proving that it holds for any variety $X$ where the effective cone of the moduli space $\mathcal{M}_g(X,\delta)$ is polyhedral for every genus $g\geq 2$ and every partition $\delta$ of $g-1$. As a consequence, we confirm the feeble Mumford hypothesis for any variety $X$ satisfying the conditions of the Conjecture of the Very Ample Cone (CVAC). Finally, we confirm the equivalence between the very strong b-principle and the strong Mumford hypothesis.

Simulating cardiac mechanics simulations is essential for understanding the organ's physiological function and pathology, yet these simulations are computationally expensive. To address this, researchers have developed various multilevel methods to accelerate linear solvers, but a comparative analysis of these conditioners is currently missing. In this work, we evaluate five multilevel strategies: two standard approaches (AMG-ML and PML), along with three recently proposed adaptive adaptive multilevel methods (AdML, AdML-2, and AdML-3). Using a viscoelastic Holzapfel-Ogden model, we assess these methods based on solver convergence, total computation time, and the coarsening of problem levels. Our findings indicate that the newly proposed adaptive methods (AdML, AdML-2, and AdML-3) offer superior performance compared to traditional conditioners.

This paper investigates random integer partitions $\lambda(\mathbf{u})$ of $\mathbf{u}=(u_1,\dots,u_k)\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}^k$, where the counts of each part size $j\in\{1,\dots,k\}$ follow independent geometric distributions. The authors derive the joint distribution of $\lambda(\mathbf{u})$'s distinct parts and their consecutive differences. Furthermore, they establish a new non-crossing division generalization of the geometric distribution's independence property for distinct parts. Finally, the paper addresses a query by Biane regarding the asymptotic behavior of the normalized distinct part counts.

Convincing video generation is a rapidly advancing technology that has garnered significant attention from both the public and researchers. This technology empowers creators to produce high-quality videos with minimal effort, effectively lowering the barrier to entry for video production. It achieves this by integrating various innovations, including text-to-video and video editing models, which have attracted widespread interest. This paper reviews the state-of-the-art models in convincing video generation, categorizing them into two main groups: those that synthesize new videos from textual descriptions and those that modify existing footage. Furthermore, it examines emerging challenges in this field and outlines potential future research avenues. Finally, we provide an accessible online resource, ConvVideoGen, which catalogs state-of-the-art models, their associated code repositories, and video samples.

This study examines the deceptive feeling of security provided by the phrase "It is impossible for it to happen." While this construction logically conveys absolute certainty, we posit that its efficacy stems from the inherent impossibility of the embedded clause "for it to happen," which allows listeners to bypass mentally simulating the event. To investigate this, we designed an experiment where participants evaluated the perceived truthfulness of sentences containing "for it to happen" versus "to happen" under conditions where the embedded proposition was either factually true or false. Results indicate that when a statement contradicts reality, the "for it to happen" phrasing generates a stronger sense of assurance compared to the standard infinitive. Furthermore, the study reveals that the presence of "for it to happen" significantly diminishes the influence of prior knowledge on truth judgments, suggesting that the syntactic structure effectively suppresses the simulation of the described event.

Acoustic metagratings are periodic surface structures designed to manipulate sound waves at a single wavelength, enabling precise control over acoustic beam steering and steering. While current acoustic metagratings typically operate at frequencies far below ultrasound, this study introduces a periodic acoustic surface featuring a minimum period of 1.2 micrometers, corresponding to a wavelength of 100 micrometers in water. Fabricated using two-photon lithography, this microacoustic metagrating successfully demonstrates first-order acoustic diffraction at 1 MHz. Furthermore, it confirms the ability to generate directional sound beams via Bragg diffraction. These results establish a pathway for creating acoustic metagratings at significantly higher frequencies, facilitating the development of miniaturized acoustic devices.

Sub-Gaussian diffusion, characterized by a probability density function that broadens more slowly than in standard Brownian motion, arises from anomalous non-Gaussian diffusion. This phenomenon occurs when a Wiener process is transformed via a deterministic, time-independent, and space-dependent mapping that involves the location's local permeability. Specifically, if permeability fluctuates randomly in space, the resulting diffusion process exhibits sub-Gaussian behavior with inherent spatial heterogeneity.

This paper presents a universal theory explaining the formation of optical patterns generated by the interaction between linear coupling and Kerr nonlinearity in one-dimensional systems. By deriving a simplified 1D coupled nonlinear Schrödinger equation (CNSE) from the coupled Maxwell-Bloch equations, the authors demonstrate that this reduced model accurately captures the dynamics of both resonator and waveguide structures. The study reveals that these optical patterns are fundamentally solitons, which can be analytically described using the inverse scattering transform. Furthermore, the work explores the formation mechanisms of various patterns, including those formed by linear coupling alone, pure Kerr nonlinearity, and their combined effects. Finally, the framework is extended to encompass coupled optical and phonon systems.

This paper introduces a novel class of regulation systems featuring unbounded controls and establishes several conversational Lyapunov theorems tailored to this framework. It is observed that systems within this category exhibit inherent unpredictability, making stochastic approaches and existing deterministic techniques largely ineffective. Consequently, we propose utilizing probabilistic contractive mappings to analyze their dynamics. Specifically, we demonstrate that if a system possesses a unique equilibrium and its trajectories converge to this point, then its associated unbounded control system admits a stochastic contractive mapping. Furthermore, we prove the converse: the existence of such a mapping, combined with appropriate stability criteria, guarantees the existence of a unique equilibrium and the asymptotic convergence of all trajectories toward it.

This study introduces a super-resolution Generative Adversarial Network (SRGAN) designed to recover high-resolution turbulent flow fields from low-resolution data. Validated using direct numerical simulation (DNS) results for turbulent channel flows at three distinct Reynolds numbers ($Re_\tau = 180, 395,$ and $590$), the proposed SRGAN framework demonstrates the ability to reconstruct fine flow structures without relying on any specific turbulence model.

This article examines three key debates regarding the wave equation: the physical interpretation of negative probability amplitudes, the validity of the correspondence principle, and the definition of quantum Zeno effects. R. D. Sorkin's analysis of a specific scenario involving two slits is central to these discussions.

Uncertainty modeling is essential for guaranteeing the reliability of AI systems, yet current methods often rely on closed environments and do not adequately address the complexities of real-life scenarios. This paper introduces a novel framework for open-world uncertainty modeling that utilizes an energy function to represent the distribution of potential outputs. By integrating an entropy-based energy function, we define an energy-driven framework that captures both aleatoric and epistemic uncertainties. We further develop an energy-driven open-world calibration method to align predicted uncertainties with true out-of-domain distributions. Experiments across multiple models and datasets demonstrate that this approach surpasses existing techniques in open-world performance.

Although significant progress has been made in applying Reinforcement Learning (RL) to real-world scenarios, the field still lacks standardized tools for benchmarking RL algorithms. To address this gap, we introduce Lif2Explorer, a new RL evaluation environment. This system offers a diverse collection of tasks spanning various difficulty levels, designed to assess both the versatility and the long-term capabilities of RL methods. Specifically, Lif2Explorer supports lifelong learning (LL) by enabling algorithms to learn multiple tasks sequentially over time. We evaluate prominent LL algorithms within this environment, demonstrating that our setup is well-suited for such assessments. Finally, we release Lif2Explorer as an open-source project on GitHub.

Declarative process management systems have emerged as a promising paradigm for orchestrating complex workflows, yet they face challenges regarding the lack of support for dynamic behaviors like failure recovery and flexible adaptations. To address this, we introduce a novel framework that integrates process management with data stream processing. By formalizing the environment surrounding a declarative process as a data stream, we enable the introduction of supervisory and recovery mechanisms through process extensions. These extensions operate as dedicated stream processors that handle interactions with the process's data flow. We demonstrate the practical application of this approach by implementing a recovery strategy for failures in a case study, formalizing it within the $\pi$-calculus to substantiate its validity.

One-dimensional photonic quasicrystals (1D-PQCs) are renowned for their ability to generate complex, nontrivial localized states within their photonic band gaps. In this study, we introduce the concept of reentrant delocalization shifts occurring in 1D-PQCs. We demonstrate that by varying the modulation strength of the aperiodic Fibonacci sequence, localized eigenmodes can transition into extended modes that penetrate into the surrounding band gap. Furthermore, we show that these reentrant modes possess tunable positions and widths, with their transition mechanisms explained through a tight-binding model.

The Lick Observatory Spectrograph (Lick Spectrograph) is a new, high-throughput, multi-object instrument installed at the Keck 1 telescope, designed to support a broad spectrum of research. This paper introduces the Data Processing System (DPS) developed for the Lick Spectrograph, which handles the entire workflow from raw data reduction to the generation of final scientific results. The DPS integrates with the standard Keck Data Management System (KDMS) and utilizes the Python programming language along with the Astropy ecosystem to ensure compatibility with existing software. Additionally, the paper outlines the software interfaces created to connect the DPS with the Target Acquisition and Guide System (TAGS) and the Keck Observatory Database (KOD).

Spatial mode demultiplexing enables the parallel analysis of individual emitters, serving as a key technique for super-resolution imaging that surpasses the optical diffraction limit. In this study, we investigate the impact of spectral crosstalk between spatial mode filters on the detection of single emitters. Our findings indicate that super-resolution capability can still be maintained even when filter crosstalk is substantial. Furthermore, we demonstrate that super-resolution imaging is achievable by utilizing the spectral features of two-photon states. Finally, we introduce a novel super-resolution method based on the spatial distribution of bi-photons, which offers a simpler and more cost-effective solution compared to traditional single-photon approaches.
This expository article explores the connections between algebraic and geometric compactifications of moduli spaces, with a specific emphasis on the moduli space of stable curves.

This study investigates population fluctuations within a two-timescale predator-prey model incorporating a Holling Type II functional response and a prey-taxis term. By analyzing a stochastic version of the system, we identify an early warning indicator for significant population shifts. Specifically, we observe that the variance of the prey population increases as it approaches extinction, serving as a signal of collapse. Furthermore, we identify a critical threshold value for the variance that marks the onset of major population changes. Numerical simulations based on the stochastic model were conducted to validate these theoretical findings.

The correlation between a galaxy's stellar mass and its star formation rate (SFR) exhibits a characteristic turnover at high masses, yet the underlying drivers remain unclear. We propose that bulges are the primary cause of this turnover, utilizing a semi-analytic model to demonstrate that the observed SFR-mass relation emerges from the interplay between bulge growth and the buildup of the stellar halo. Specifically, massive galaxies form their bulges through major mergers, which simultaneously trigger intense starbursts and deplete the gas reservoirs. Consequently, the turnover in the M*-SFR relation at elevated masses is attributed to the timescale required for bulge formation, rather than the timescale of gas consumption.

We introduce Self-Invalidation and Self-Devaluation, two novel comparison-based sorting algorithms. Self-Invalidation operates by having elements invalidate their own comparisons, while Self-Devaluation involves elements comparing themselves only to those with lower scores. Both methods achieve a comparison count of $O(n \log n)$, where $n$ represents the total number of elements.

Let $A$ be a finite subset within an abelian group such that $|A + A| \leq d|A|$. Freiman's 3k-4 theorem, established by the author, demonstrates that if $3|A + A| < 4$, then $A$ is contained in a generalized arithmetic progression whose length does not exceed $d|A|$. This paper improves upon Freiman's 3k-4 theorem by proving that if $2|A + A| < 3$, then $A$ lies within a generalized arithmetic progression of length at most $d|A + A|$. Consequently, this improved result allows for the strengthening of the Green-Tao theorem, which originally showed that the primes contain arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions; the new finding implies that any $D$-dense subset of an infinite abelian group also contains arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions.

A Dirac-style time-dependent variational approach is applied to the H\'enon-Heles model, utilizing a complex spinor ansatz and the Jackiw-Kerman functional. This application yields two distinct quantum chaotic scenarios. In the first scenario, quantum effects stabilize an oscillatory ansatz solution, causing it to persist even when the classical system exhibits chaos. Conversely, the second scenario involves a quantum ansatz solution that undergoes destabilization, allowing underlying quantum chaos to emerge despite the classical H\'enon-Heiles model being integrable.

This study explores the potential of analyzing X-ray images to identify traits that predict whether a COVID-19 patient will require ICU admission. We hypothesize that specific features within these images correlate with the need for intensive care. To test this, we utilized a dataset of 1,000 X-ray images from 500 patients, split evenly between those who were discharged without ICU care and those who needed ICU admission. We employed a ResNet-50 model, pre-trained on ImageNet, to extract deep features from the images. We then applied a Random Forest classifier to these features to determine if ICU-requiring patients exhibit distinct characteristics compared to those who were not. Results indicate that ResNet-50 successfully extracted meaningful features, and the Random Forest classifier achieved an accuracy of 0.60. This suggests that ICU admission needs may be discernible from X-ray imaging, potentially offering a valuable non-invasive diagnostic tool.

The classical result by Whitehead establishes that the fiber of a simplicial group bundle is itself a simplicial group. This paper extends that finding to cover the broader framework of simplicial set bundles.

Visual relationship detection (VRD) serves as a vital yet under-explored task within human-centric scene understanding, aiming to identify interactions between individuals and objects. A significant obstacle in VRD is the high rate of false detections, primarily caused by ambiguous visual cues and noisy background elements. To address this, we introduce a novel framework called CREDIBLE, designed to enhance the precision of visual relationship triples. Our approach consists of two key modules: the first, the Coarse Filter, eliminates low-confidence detections by identifying and removing noisy samples, while the second, the Refinement Module, sharpens the accuracy of remaining candidates through a two-stage process. Initially, it employs a coarse detector to predict potential object pairs and their interactions, followed by a fine-tuned detector that leverages these contextual pair predictions to improve individual instance accuracy. Experiments on the Visual Genome and HRS datasets demonstrate that CREDRED significantly surpasses current state-of-the-art methods.

Activity recognition systems are frequently hindered by factors such as insufficient illumination, limited visual information, and constrained datasets. To address these challenges, we introduce Delta Sampling R-Net, a lightweight activity recognition framework that utilizes temporal delta sampling to process video inputs. This approach samples frames based on the time intervals between them rather than a fixed frequency, allowing the system to capture high-frequency movements with greater detail while reducing data volume during periods of inactivity. Additionally, we propose a restricted activity recognition framework that leverages this efficient sampling strategy to enhance performance on small-scale datasets and in dimly lit environments. Experimental results demonstrate that Delta Sampling R-Net achieves performance comparable to the original R-Net on the standard ActivityNet 1.3 dataset. However, on a newly created dataset featuring low-light and restricted data conditions, Delta Sampling R-Net surpasses the original R-Net, improving mean Average Precision (mAP) by 11.1%.

Concurrent processing is a well-established technique for enhancing computational performance, typically realized through specialized hardware like GPUs or via data-parallel instruction sets (e.g., OpenMP, CUDA, or CL). However, current hardware implementations often demand highly structured and uniform data layouts, which can restrict their applicability to problems with irregular data access patterns. This paper introduces a novel approach to executing process-level parallelism on hardware that accommodates irregular data structures. The suggested method utilizes a unified global address space, enabling processors to retrieve and store data using standard address-based operations. This is achieved by deploying a Data Addressable Memory (DAM) subsystem built upon a network-on-chip (NoC) architecture. This subsystem provides sufficient bandwidth and bandwidth to support the concurrent read and write operations of multiple processors simultaneously. Furthermore, this Data Addressable Memory subsystem is designed to be lightweight, requiring minimal FPGA resources. The host halo ($M_{200} = 10^{13} M_{\odot}$) contains a stellar disk ($M_{\star} = 10^{11} M_{\odot}$) exhibiting significant lopsidedness ($|a_2/a_0| = 0.4$), while the satellite is a gas disk ($M_{\rm gas} = 10^{10} M_{\odot}$) with a central surface density of $10 M_{\odot} \rm pc^{-2}$. The satellite's orbit is retrograde and inclined at 60 degrees, leading to a prolonged, off-center interaction. This event triggers a burst of star formation ($\sim 10^9 M_{\odot} \rm yr^{-1}$) in the satellite's core, which merges into the disk after approximately 3.5 billion years. The resulting galaxy retains its lopsided structure but develops a central bulge ($M_{\rm bulge} = 10^{10} M_{\odot}$) that remains off-center. The concept of Global Structure Flavours (FSZ) has long served as a compelling theoretical framework for explaining the hierarchy of fermion masses and mixing angles. This framework relies on a flavour symmetry group, $G_F$, which is spontaneously broken down to the product of baryon number ($B$) and the standard model gauge group ($G_{SM}$). This breaking mechanism generates both flavour and CP-violating phenomena. In this study, we investigate the phenomenology of Global FSZ by conducting a comprehensive scan of the model's parameter space using Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MHC) methods. This analysis incorporates diverse experimental constraints, including precision electroweak data, direct searches for new physics, flavour observables, and cosmological limits. Our findings indicate that the model remains viable, with the most recent Higgs diphoton decay measurements playing a pivotal role in shaping the allowed parameter regions. Furthermore, we identify specific areas within the allowed space capable of generating detectable deviations in the $B$-meson mixing phase, $\phi_s$, and the electric dipole moments of the muon and electron.

We examine a nonlinear elliptic equation defined on $\mathbb{R}^2$, featuring a locally compact perturbation of critical Hardy-Sobolev type. Our analysis reveals that localized bubbling solutions occur exclusively at points of minimal energy for the embedding's best constant, which is localized within the potential. Furthermore, we establish precise asymptotic behavior for blow-up profiles at blow-up centers where the potential is strictly positive.

We introduce a neural framework for code generation that incorporates static evaluation. In this approach, a neural model produces a candidate code snippet, which is subsequently refined via static analysis to eliminate potential errors. The model is trained using a reinforcement learning strategy where the reward is determined by the success of the final modified code in executing within its target environment. This framework is designed to address three specific challenges: generating function bodies, constructing while-loop bodies, and synthesizing complete Python programs. The proposed system is evaluated against three datasets, demonstrating that it outperforms state-of-the-art methods by a significant margin.

On November 7, 2004, a significant solar neutron event occurred, characterized by a notable increase in neutron flux originating from the Sun. This event was driven by a solar flare of X-ray class X1.8, accompanied by a coronal mass ejection (CME). The analysis of this event indicates that the peak neutron flux reached approximately $10^8$ neutrons per square centimeter per second, with the peak lasting roughly 10 minutes. The findings suggest that the primary cause of this intense neutron emission was the acceleration of protons by the associated electromagnetic fields.

This study investigates the dispersion equations for both Newtonian and non-Newtonian viscous hydrodynamics, focusing on their linearized forms. It is demonstrated that the Newtonian linearization yields a single linear dispersion equation, whereas the non-Newtonian approach necessitates a system composed of two linear dispersion equations. Furthermore, it is shown that the standard linear dispersion equation associated with the non-Newtonian framework can be derived directly from this newly formulated system of two equations.

Anomaly detection is a critical task in data analysis, yet existing methods often struggle with the inherent complexity of quantum measurement processes. To address this, we introduce **In-Game Quantum Measurement Anomaly Detection (InQMAD)**, a new framework designed to identify irregularities in quantum measurements. In this approach, an adversary injects a malicious quantum state into the system to cause deviations in the honest party's measurement outcomes. We define the anomaly as the statistical divergence between the honest party's state when interacting with the adversary versus a standard honest interaction. Our solution employs a two-stage strategy: first, a modified version of the Johnsen-Mandelbrot algorithm identifies a suspicious state through a single measurement, and second, the protocol verifies this state using multiple copies to confirm the anomaly. We demonstrate that InQMAD achieves a constant success probability in detecting such anomalies while utilizing a minimal number of qudits.

In an era where digital coercion is increasingly prevalent, ensuring individuals retain control over their personal data is paramount. This study examines a scenario in which a coercing party forces a decryption key provider to reveal a plaintext from ciphertext, aiming to determine if verification mechanisms can be established to prevent such attacks. We introduce a generic framework for decryption verification that accommodates various cryptographic primitives and demonstrates its application to both symmetric and public-key settings. Furthermore, we investigate the feasibility of constructing zero-knowledge proofs within this model to ensure the decryptor cannot leverage the verification process to learn the plaintext.

We introduce a universal framework for modeling measurement-device-independent quantum key exchange (MDI-QKX) protocols, applicable to any linear optics setup. This approach enables the simulation of an entire round of an MDI-QKX protocol, including the generation of random pulses by source modules, the evolution of multi-photon wavepackets through linear optics, and the detection events at single-photon modules. The generated random bit stream is then processed to calculate the final shared secret key. The utility of this framework is demonstrated by simulating three distinct MDI-QKX protocols: the variants proposed by Lo et al., by Wang et al., and the one introduced by the authors themselves.

This paper introduces a novel numerical approach for solving Fokker-Planck equations, which govern the evolution of probability densities in average field games. The proposed method integrates a time-stepping scheme with a spatial discretization technique. Spatially, it combines a Lagrange-Galer framework with a weak time derivative, whereas temporally it employs a high-order Lagrange-Galer scheme. The authors derive a priori estimates for the method and establish convergence results for the weak time derivative within a specific Sobolev space. Furthermore, the paper demonstrates how to reconstruct the solution's gradient using a post-processing strategy. Finally, it presents numerical experiments that validate the theoretical findings and verify the observed convergence rates.

Deep neural networks (DNNs) have become the leading approach for numerous machine learning tasks, yet their functioning remains largely opaque. This study investigates how DNNs process input data, specifically examining the visual patterns of activation maps within fully connected layers. We conducted experiments on the MNIST dataset to analyze these internal representations. Furthermore, we evaluated human ability to comprehend these maps through two distinct tasks: a naming exercise and an classification challenge. Our findings indicate that humans can successfully identify MNIST digits using only the network's activation maps, achieving an accuracy of approximately 95%.

Planetary ingestion is hypothesized to account for the rapid rotation observed in some young stars, yet current evidence remains inconclusive. We present new findings from a suite of 3D hydrodynamic simulations that track the aftermath of a planet colliding with a star. Our results indicate that the rotation of the stellar remnant depends heavily on the nature of the post-impact interaction. If the planet merges entirely with the star, the resulting object spins only moderately faster than pre-impact levels. Conversely, if the impact creates a temporary, distinct accretion disk that separates the planet's material from the star, the system can achieve extreme rotation speeds. This latter scenario implies that the planet's angular momentum must be partially deposited into the disk rather than the star itself.

The proliferation of fake news across social media platforms poses a significant threat to public safety and societal stability. Fake news is characterized by its ability to spread rapidly and generate substantial harm, often leveraging emotional content and multimodal elements such as text and images to deceive readers. While existing detection methods have achieved notable success, they frequently rely on rigid, handcrafted feature engineering and fail to adequately capture the complex, cross-modal interactions inherent in false news. To address these shortcomings, we propose a novel meta neural process framework designed for emergent fake news identification. This approach utilizes a probabilistic meta-learning strategy to automatically learn the latent correlations between different modalities, thereby capturing intricate multimodal patterns without manual intervention. Extensive experiments conducted on two benchmark datasets demonstrate that our method significantly surpasses state-of-the-art detection models.

This study examines a discrete time status refresh mechanism involving an infinite horizon, where the system age is defined as the interval since the most recent update. In each time slot, a potential update opportunity occurs with probability $p$; upon realization, the system age resets to one slot, whereas it simply increments by one if no update happens. We analyze two scenarios based on the information content of updates: (i) updates convey no new information, and (ii) updates provide information valid for exactly one time slot. For both cases, we derive the optimal policy that minimizes the long-term expected age of information (EOI), along with its corresponding steady-state information freshness metrics, specifically the average age and the average packet error rate. We further investigate the optimal policy for information-bearing updates under the assumption of a Bernoulli/Single-Server/Loss/1 queue. In this context, we establish the optimality of a $(Q, \text{threshold})$ type policy and determine the long-term expected age of information via a specific formula. Finally, we examine the scenario where the update opportunity probability $p$ is contingent upon the current system age.

A. V. Mikhailov previously demonstrated that set-theoretic regular set solutions of the Yang-Baxter equation yield a quasi-triangular quasi-quantum Yang-Baxter algebra structure. In this paper, we generalize this finding by proving that any finite set solution of the Yang-Baxter equation is sufficient to construct a quasi-bialgebra.
This paper presents a method for generating Golay complementary pairs of multiphase $L$-tuples, where each element has a size of $k \times L$.

Silicon's robust material attributes, including its exceptional stability, scalability, and mature fabrication infrastructure, make it an ideal candidate for quantum computing. However, realizing this potential requires overcoming the challenge of introducing and manipulating stable, long-lived quantum states within the silicon lattice. This study demonstrates that a Si/SiGe quantum dot can host a stable, controllable intervalley interaction between two electron spins. By leveraging this interaction, we successfully execute a two-qubit valley swap gate with high fidelity ($0.99$) and execute single-spin rotations ($0.99$) via spin transfer. These results establish a pathway for silicon-based spin-valley quantum processors.

Complex systems, characterized by their intricate web of interactions, often defy analysis through traditional methods. To address this, we propose a novel framework that leverages Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to model the temporal evolution of complex systems. In this approach, the system's state is represented as a graph, where GNNs generate embeddings that encapsulate the dynamics of the system's components. We validate our method on two distinct datasets: the human brain and the human body. Our findings demonstrate that our framework can accurately predict the next state of the brain and the physiological condition of the body, even when the input data is incomplete. Furthermore, we utilize these predictions to uncover hidden structural patterns within the networks.

In the study of division rings within the stable homotopy category of a prime characteristic $p$, we derive enumerations for their divisions by leveraging the fact that any division ring's unit group must be a Bott periodicity line. Our findings indicate that, up to isomorphism, division rings exist only in degrees $0$ and $1$, with their endomorphism algebras identified as the truncated polynomial algeens $H\mathbb{F}_p$ and $k\mathbb{F}_p$ (where $k$ denotes the degree of the Bott element), respectively.

Adversarial neural networks have recently been utilized to create synthetic medical images that support data augmentation. However, these models often require substantial amounts of real images for training, which can be difficult to obtain for rare pathologies. To address this limitation, we introduce a new framework for generating synthetic MR images of brain lesions using a Progressive Adversarial Variational Auto-Encoder (PA-VAE). This model employs a two-stage approach: initially, a VAE is trained to capture the structural features of healthy brain scans, and subsequently, this encoder is integrated into an adversarial system for fine-tuning. In the second phase, the model is trained on a dataset containing both normal images and those with lesions. Our method was evaluated using T1-weighted MRI data from the ADNI repository, which includes scans of healthy individuals and those with Alzheimer's disease. The results indicate that our proposed approach outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in enhancing the accuracy of Alzheimer's classification tasks.

Quantum steering represents a robust form of nonlocality that has garnered significant attention, particularly regarding its application in characterizing multipartite systems. In this study, we introduce a novel class of local operations termed "Local Operations within the Unextendible Product Framework" (LUP), which generalizes the standard Local Operations and Classical Communication (LOCC) by defining an unextendible product operator framework. We demonstrate that HSWAP operations constitute a specific subset of LUP. Furthermore, we establish a criterion asserting that quantum steering remains robust even when subjected to robust local operations of the LUP type. Specifically, we examine robustness in the context of the HSWAP framework and derive a necessary and sufficient condition for robust quantum steering under these operations. Finally, we investigate the scenario involving the framework of unextendible product bases (UPB) across heterogeneous systems.

The fifth iteration of the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS-V) relies on a coordinated effort between two telescopes, a strategy designed to enhance the survey's scope and efficiency. This paper outlines the experimental validation of the autonomous coordination system employed in SDSS-V, which integrates the Robotic Optical Telescopes in Europe (ROTEC) and the Robotic 2-meter Telescope (R2T) located at Calar Alto Observatory in Spain. These experiments were conducted at the European Organization for Nuclear Research (CERN) in Geneva, Switzerland, where R2T was temporarily relocated to the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) tunnel. The study confirms the feasibility of fully secure coordination, demonstrating that the LHC's magnetic field does not degrade the optical performance of R2T or its ability to coordinate with ROTEC. Furthermore, the research establishes that the LHC environment serves as a viable site for future robotic optical experiments.

We introduce Feature Extraction via Comparative Learning (FECL), a unified framework designed to enhance the performance of various feature extraction methods. Within FECL, a feature extractor is defined as a function mapping an input image to a set of features, where features are optimized by comparing feature maps generated from positive and negative samples. This approach offers two primary advantages: it streamlines feature optimization by consolidating multiple methods into a single framework, and it significantly accelerates training by reducing the number of required positive images per batch. Empirical evaluations on the CUB-200-2011 and Visual Genome datasets confirm that FECL outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques. Source code is accessible at https://github.com/zhengzj1992/FECL.

This paper introduces a novel family of finite star normal quotient diagrams, denoted as $D_n$, which exhibit twisted wreath type with degree parameters $d_1 = d_2 = 2$ and $d_3 = n+1$, where $n \ge 2$ is an integer. It is established that each diagram $D_n$ yields a dually hyperbolic torsion-free quotient diagram $Q_n$ possessing a finitely generated fundamental group. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that these families $\{Q_n\}_{n \ge 2}$ are pairwise non-isomorphic.

This paper introduces a novel approach for modeling high-dimensional nominal data, addressing a gap as existing methods typically ignore interactions among levels of nominal variables or treat them as independent. We propose a new framework that incorporates group structures to enhance sparsity and interpretability. Specifically, we define a new penalty function that simultaneously captures sparsity and encodes the inherent hierarchy of nominal data. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that this method achieves superior performance compared to current state-of-the-art techniques.

Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable general capabilities, yet integrating structured knowledge—such as knowledge graphs (KGs)—remains challenging. This integration is crucial for enhancing reasoning, enabling fact-based responses, and correcting hallucinations. We introduce **ABILITY** (Structured Knowledge Integration for Large Language Models), a novel framework designed to generate high-quality outputs by leveraging graph-based knowledge. Our approach employs a multi-stage strategy: first, it extracts relevant information from the target KG using a specialized graph encoder; subsequently, it refines the user query and synthesizes the final answer by combining this extracted knowledge with the original query through a specialized graph-enhanced prompt. We evaluated our method on two datasets, **L-KBQA** and **MedQA**, covering general and medical domains. Our results indicate that ABILITY significantly surpasses existing state-of-the-art techniques, achieving a +10.5 improvement in F1 score on L-KBQA and +13.1 on MedQA.

Panoramic stitching merges multiple overlapping images into a single wide view, a technique widely used in virtual reality and robotics. Although various methods exist, they often yield results with discontinuities at seams, which can cause motion sickness in users exposed to them. To address this, we propose a new approach that integrates known information about human perception of motion, specifically the vestibular system's sensitivity to acceleration. By modeling this using a linear dynamical system, we introduce a novel optimization framework that generates smoothest possible trajectories based on available data and prior knowledge. This method yields a smooth path through the scene, which is then rendered via view synthesis. Experiments demonstrate that our method outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques, significantly reducing viewer discomfort.

Developing computational models of Parkinson's disease (PD) is essential for advancing our understanding of its pathophysiology and for creating new therapies. However, a significant obstacle remains: accurately modeling the complex interplay between neural and non-neural factors that drive PD. To address this, we propose a novel biophysical model of the basal ganglia that integrates extensive experimental data from marmoset primates. This approach allows us to simulate the effects of dopamine depletion on the motor symptoms characteristic of PD. Furthermore, the model provides a theoretical basis for investigating the efficacy of deep brain stimulation (DBS) as a treatment.

Spatial anti-aliasing is essential for rendering smooth line junctions on maps, yet it remains a significant challenge because the visual appearance of these areas depends on multiple factors, including the geometry of the line network, the map's zoom level, and the viewing angle. To address this, we introduce a novel rendering technique that dynamically calculates an adaptive anti-aliasing width. This approach accounts for the geometric complexity of junctions, zoom level, and perspective. Evaluations demonstrate that this method produces highly realistic results across diverse map configurations while maintaining superior performance.

We present IFU observations of nine nearby Ultra/Luminous Infrared Galaxies (U/LIRGs) at redshifts $z < 0.04$ as part of the KOOLS-IFU project, utilizing the Seimei Telescope. This sample represents the first integral field spectroscopic survey of U/LIRGs conducted with the KOOLS-IFU instrument. The dataset includes eight galaxies with effective radii ($R_{\rm eff}$) exceeding 1.5 kpc and one galaxy with $R_{\rm eff} = 0.5$ kpc. We employed the Bayesian code FIREFLY to derive kinematic parameters, specifically circular velocity ($V_c$), inclination ($i$), and position angle (PA), for each system. Our findings reveal that the sample exhibits a wide range of $V_c$ values between 30 and 250 km s$^{-1}$, with a median velocity of 110 km s$^{-1}$. The observed median inclination is 60 degrees ($\sigma=16^\circ$), while the median PA is 110 degrees ($\sigma=20^\circ$). Furthermore, we identified a correlation between $V_c$ and the [C ii] 158 $\mu$m emission line flux, suggesting that the distribution of circumnuclear gas in these U/LIRGs is linked to their central black hole accretion processes.
